lead: An app can send a short message without owning a radio stack. On Android, SmsManager hands text to the phone's SMS service; e-mail goes through an intent to a mail app. This keeps account setup, retries and carrier billing outside your code. Apps use it for OTP alerts, delivery updates, support replies, UPI receipts and sharing invoices. Some syllabi call it SMS messaging and sending e-mail.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 intents and built-in apps, and Unit 1 SMS as a mobile service.

blocks.text: SmsManager is the Android class that talks to the telephony service. Declare the SEND_SMS permission in the manifest and request SEND_SMS at runtime on Android 6.0 and later. Without it, the call throws SecurityException.

A single 7-bit GSM SMS carries 160 characters. A long message is concatenated: each part carries a user data header of 6 bytes, and after 7-bit packing that header takes 7 of the 160 characters, leaving 153 characters of payload per part (160 − 7 = 153). Use divideMessage(text), which returns a list of strings already split at safe boundaries. Do not cut at 160 yourself.

items: Call SmsManager sms = SmsManager.getDefault(). On API 31 and later use context.getSystemService(SmsManager.class), which also supports per-SIM managers; getDefault() is deprecated from Android 12 (API 31).
Build a sent PendingIntent and a delivered PendingIntent for each part.
For each part call sms.sendTextMessage(phone, null, part, sentPI, deliveredPI).
Check the result code in the sent receiver; handle RESULT_ERROR_GENERIC_FAILURE and RESULT_ERROR_RADIO_OFF.

blocks.text: The sent intent fires when the part leaves the phone for the carrier. The delivered intent fires when the recipient's phone acknowledges it. Billing is per part, so a 320-character message is three chargeable SMS. Keep the destination in E.164 form, for example +919876543210.

Your app does not log in to an SMTP server. It asks a mail app to compose. For an e-mail-only action use Intent.ACTION_SENDTO with a mailto: URI. For general sharing use Intent.ACTION_SEND with type text/plain and wrap it in Intent.createChooser.

For ACTION_SENDTO put the address in the URI, for example Uri.parse("mailto:someone@example.com"); EXTRA_EMAIL is not reliable there and some mail apps ignore it. EXTRA_EMAIL is used when you attach recipients to ACTION_SEND or ACTION_SEND_MULTIPLE. Other fields go in extras: EXTRA_SUBJECT, EXTRA_TEXT for body, and EXTRA_STREAM for an attachment. An attachment must be a content:// URI, not file://; add FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION so the mail app can read it.

The chooser shows every app that can handle the intent. With createChooser the chooser itself shows its own message when no app matches. The try/catch for ActivityNotFoundException is needed when you start ACTION_SENDTO, or any implicit intent, directly without a chooser. The user still taps Send inside the mail app, so your app never sees the final message.
E-mail needs a configured account and internet; SMS needs carrier signal and balance. Test on a real phone: emulators often lack a SIM and a mail account.

spec.aria: A bar of 320 characters split into three parts of 153, 153 and 14 characters, each with a small header block and a price of 0.20 rupees, totalling 0.60 rupees.

examples.question: An Android app sends a 320-character SMS in 7-bit GSM encoding. A single SMS carries 160 characters. Each part of a concatenated SMS carries 153 characters because the 6-byte user data header takes 7 characters of the 160. How many SMS parts are sent? At ₹0.20 per part, what is the cost?
examples.answer: 3 SMS parts are sent; the cost is ₹0.60.
examples.check:
import math
L = 320
per = 153
parts = math.ceil(L / per)
cost = parts * 0.20
print(parts)
print(round(cost, 2))

traps: Using 160 characters per part for a long SMS; the 6-byte concatenation header takes 7 characters, leaving 153 characters per part in 7-bit GSM.
Treating the sent PendingIntent as proof of delivery; sent means handed to the carrier, delivered means the recipient phone acknowledged.
Forgetting the runtime SEND_SMS permission and getting SecurityException.
Using ACTION_SEND when only e-mail apps should answer; ACTION_SENDTO with a mailto: URI restricts the chooser to e-mail.
Passing a file:// attachment; use a content:// URI with FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION.

quiz.q: Which Android permission is required to call SmsManager.sendTextMessage?
Why does divideMessage use 153 characters per part, not 160?
quiz.a: A concatenated SMS carries a 6-byte user data header; after 7-bit packing the header takes 7 of the 160 characters, leaving 153 characters of payload per part in 7-bit GSM.

quiz.q: A 400-character 7-bit SMS is split at 153 characters per part. How many parts, and at ₹0.25 per part what is the cost?
An app gets a sent result but no delivery result. Which PendingIntent is missing, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: The delivered PendingIntent is missing. It fires only when the recipient's phone acknowledges the message; the sent intent only shows handoff to the carrier.

quiz.q: Which intent sends e-mail only to a chosen address?
quiz.a: Intent.ACTION_SENDTO with a mailto: URI carrying the address.

quiz.q: State one difference between ACTION_SENDTO and ACTION_SEND.
quiz.a: ACTION_SENDTO targets a URI scheme such as mailto: and limits handlers; ACTION_SEND shares content by MIME type and may show many apps.

quiz.q: Which extra carries an attachment, and what URI scheme should it use?
Why wrap an e-mail intent in createChooser?
quiz.a: The chooser lets the user pick among mail apps and gives a clear fallback when several apps match; the app does not need to know the user's mail app.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production apps often avoid direct SMS for OTP and use the SMS Retriever API or push messages, because SEND_SMS is a sensitive permission. RCS, WhatsApp Business and e-mail APIs handle richer messages. Search for Android SMS Retriever, SmsManager delivery reports, ACTION_SENDTO, FileProvider and RCS.
